series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a folio into the LRU (Least Recently Used) list out of the swap cache allocator function. The reason for this change is that zswap writeback requires a swap cache folio that can be freed directly once writeback completes, without being on the LRU. The patch introduces a new function __swap_cache_alloc_folio() that allocates a folio but does not add it to the LRU, allowing the caller to manage its lifecycle. This change is intended to be functional equivalent to the original code and only affects how the LRU is handled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's swap management to drop PG_dropbehind folios from the swap cache immediately after writeback completion, rather than waiting for reclaim to find them later. This is achieved by introducing a new function, swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio(), which is called when writeback completes and frees the folios in batches. The patch also updates various functions to use this new function and adds necessary locking mechanisms to ensure thread safety. The goal of this change is to improve performance by reducing the time spent on reclaiming swap cache folios.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the zswap writeback process by allocating a folio off the LRU and marking it for dropbehind, allowing the swap cache to free it once writeback completes. This reduces memory waste and minimizes the time cold pages remain resident. The approach taken is to modify the zswap_writeback_entry function to set the PG_dropbehind flag on the allocated folio.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series improves memory management for zswap by freeing cold writeback folios promptly, rather than leaving them on the LRU for page reclaim to find and free later. It achieves this by extending the existing dropbehind mechanism to swap cache folios and having zswap opt into it. The patches move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator, drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion, and modify zswap to allocate its writeback folio off the LRU and mark it dropbehind. This reduces memory waste and keeps cold memory resident for a shorter period.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the madvise_free_huge_pmd() function to skip zone device folios when performing lazyfree operations. The existing guards in this function do not cover all cases of zone device memory, and adding a check for zone device folios ensures that these areas are properly handled. This change addresses an issue where THP migration of zone device pages was not being filtered correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/madvise: skip zone device folios in cold/pageout PMD range
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a bug in the madvise_cold_or_pageout_pte_range function, which incorrectly ages or reclaims zone device memory. The fix involves skipping ZONE_DEVICE folios during MADV_COLD/PAGEOUT operations.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses the issue of stale memory cgroup (memcg) stats causing premature OOM kills by proposing a solution to reduce the overhead of updating and flushing these statistics. The idea is for memcg to accumulate updates on a per-CPU basis, then propagate them up to a global atomic counter when it reaches a certain threshold, eliminating the need for frequent flushing. This approach aims to scale better for large machines with many cores and focuses on reducing the number of stats that require flushing, specifically NR_FILE_DIRTY and NR_WRITEBACK in the writeback case.

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Yosry Ahmed noted that the patch may not address premature OOM kills due to stale stats in the vmscan path, citing a test where VMs experienced OOM kills after the ratelimited flush, and suggested further investigation is needed.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed questioned the trade-off between update and read performance in memcg stats, suggesting that increasing the cost of updates could improve the manageability of the read path, which is becoming slow in some cases.

The reviewer pointed out that memcg stats perform similar per-CPU counting and thresholding as vmstat, but with a cgroup hierarchy, which requires reading hierarchical stats including children. They suggested replacing the current flushing logic with updating the stat on each parent or forgoing the rstat flushing logic altogether.

Reviewer suggested side-stepping the flushing issue by either keeping track of CPUs with updates via rstat or propagating per-CPU stat updates when reaching a threshold, similar to how vmstat handles batching
review_comments.raw_body:
I don't think we had time to look into this closely. We have a test
that runs VMs with some memory pressure / reclaim, and we observed OOM
kills in that test after the ratelimited flush in the vmscan path.
Whether or not this translates to additional OOM kills in our prod is
currently unknown, but it's a signal that reclaim effectiveness may be
negatively affected in some cases.

---

Yeah I think we generally want to keep updates faster than reads,
because some of them are also in latency-sensitive paths like
networking. However, since reads are becoming too slow in some cases,
the question here is whether we can afford some extra cost on the
update side (to iterate parent per-CPU counters) to make the read path
more manageable.

---

The memcg stats perform similar per-CPU counting and thresholding. The
main difference from vmstat AFAICT is the cgroup hierarchy. In vmstat
we have per-CPU counters and a global atomic counter for each stat.
For memcg, we have the same for each cgroup, then we also have a
cgroup tree. When we read the stats of a cgroup, we usually want the
hierarchical stats including all of its children, so we can't just
read the global counter.

We use rstat, a cgroup framework that keeps track of which cgroups
have updates on which CPUs, and then memcg has thresholding logic on
top to only flush if the number of pending updates exceeds a
threshold. Essentially, if the magnitude updates on a CPU exceeds
MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH, we add it to a global per-memcg counter. We only
flush if that global per-memcg counter has > NR_CPUS *
MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH updates. So in theory I think we tolerate up to 2 *
NR_CPUS * MEMCG_CHARGE_BATCH of stale stats (combined for all the
stats).

See memcg_rstat_updated() and memcg_vmstats_needs_flush() for this logic.

Looking at this code again, it made me realize that we already iterate
the per-CPU stats_updates on every update to increment the number of
pending stats on this CPU. I wonder if we can replace this with
actually updating the stat on each parent, then the flush path only
needs to accumulate CPU counters. Or maybe as you mention, we update
the global per-memcg counter when updates on a CPU exceed a threshold,
and forgo the rstat flushing logic completely.

---

Probably not (hence I called it radical), but I think this can be
side-stepped by either keeping the tracking of CPUs that have updates
via rstat (or similar), or just propagating the per-CPU stat updates
when they reach a threshold like vmstat.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing concerns about the performance impact of flushing memcg stats and exploring an alternative approach to batching updates. She proposes running experiments to test updating global per-memcg counters in batches, but notes that this may incur a nontrivial performance hit due to unconditional walking of ancestors on every update.
review_comments.raw_body:
I can run some experiments and see if updating the global per-memcg
counter per batch and forgoing flushing could be a viable solution. I
can use my setup to test it for writeback, but for the zswap use case,
what's the best way to test if the changes are too expensive? Is there
a benchmark program you're running?

For updating the stat on each parent and having the flush path only
accumulate CPU counters, I think this means we would have to
unconditionally walk the ancestors + update its counters on every
update, as we wouldn't be able to early break if the flushable
threshold was already exceeded. I don't think we could replace the
stats_update update, as it seems like readers still need some way of
knowing when to flush. It seems like this could be a nontrivial
performance hit, but maybe it's a non-factor in reality. If you think
this would be useful to get benchmark numbers on, I can run some
experiments on this too.

Thanks,
Joanne

review_comments.author: Yosry Ahmed
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer suggested that memcg could use a batching approach similar to vmstat, where the per-CPU counter is accumulated and propagated up to a global atomic counter only when it reaches a threshold, potentially eliminating the need for flushing.

Reviewer Yosry Ahmed suggested experimenting with shifting workload between update and reader sides for memcg stats flushing, proposing two options: (a) updating per-CPU counters directly on stats updates or (b) using a global atomic counter that's updated when the per-CPU threshold is exceeded. He also proposed running benchmarks to test worst-case scenarios.
review_comments.raw_body:
I was running stress-ng and measuring the latency of zswap_load() and
zswap_store() with bpftrace. But I suspect whatever works for writeback
should work for zswap :)

---

I think we need to experiment with how much work we can shift around
between the update and reader sides.

Right now, on the update side, we call __css_rstat_updated(), which
iterates the parents and puts them on the per-CPU rstat tree, then we
iterate the parents again in memcg_rstat_updated() and:
- Check if flushing threshold is already met.
- Update per-CPU counter for stats_updates.
- If per-CPU update exceeds (another) threshold, we update an atomic for
  stats_updates.

The flush side checks the flushing threshold and does an rstat flush,
which will walk the update trees on all CPUs and iterates all child
cgroups on it. Pretty expensive when the threshold is met.

I think we discussed two different options:

(a) On stats updates, iterate the parents and update the per-CPU
counters of the stat directly.

In this case, we can't keep using rstat, as we would still need to add
the cgroup and all its ancestors to the update tree anyway and the flush
cost will remain similar. So on the flush path we'll need to iterate all
CPUs and add the counters. We can explore if use a cpumask can help
here, but perhaps not since we'll need to update it atomically on all
stat updates.

I imagine that if we do this we'll drop the stats_updates optimization
to avoid adding more cost to the update side. We'll be replacing parent
stats_updates modification with parent stat counter modification. But
maybe it's feasible to keep both to limit the cost of flusing.

This only works if the cost of iterate the CPUs on the flush side ends
up being cheaper than the current flush. I imagine the average cost will
be higher but the cost should be much more consistent vs the current
flush, so the tail should be better.

(b) On stats updates, iterate the parents and update the per-CPU
counters of the stat directly AND update a global atomic if the per-CPU
counter exceeds a threshold. I think updates may get too expensive as we
may need to update multiple atomics, especially when updating the root
counter as it will be contended by all cgroups.

The flush side becomes an atomic read, so should be very cheap, and we
can drop other heuristics and optimizations.

---

I think ultimately we need to experiment with these approachs (and
perhaps others) to check what actually works in practice. You'll
probably want some benchmarks or synthetic tests with many cgroups to
exercise the worst case scenarios.

For the zswap stats, I used to run stress-ng with a bunch of workers
(20, 50, 100, ..) in cgroups of different levels. Since all workers are
in the same cgroups, all the parents are common and all threads end up
competing on the same atomics, so worst case scenario. I was also
testing in a VM that has more CPUs than stress-ng workers, to exercise
the full extent of the concurrency and contention.

This could be a lot of work, so I am not really asking you to do it, but
just brainstorming and sharing ideas :)

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author Joanne Koong addressed Yosry Ahmed's concern about the impact of stale stats on various kernel components, specifically zswap, cachestat(), working set, and vmscan. She performed armchair analysis for each component, concluding that only vmscan is troublesome due to its reliance on accurate stats to determine whether reclaim can deactivate. Joanne acknowledged the potential issue in vmscan but did not propose a fix, instead suggesting that frequent flushing might not solve the problem and proposing alternative solutions such as keeping deactivation state for a period of time if refaults were observed.
sentiment_signals: acknowledged potential issue but no proposed fix
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for your guidance and insights on this, Yosry! Your responses
have been very helpful.

I'll do some experimentation with this and try to get a sense of what
the update costs are.

One thing I was unclear about and have been looking at is how
pervasive/important this issue is outside of the writeback case. It
looks like there are roughly 4 other categories of users that rely on
stats that can be 2s stale: zswap, cachestat(), working set, and
vmscan.

Of these, vmscan is the only one that looks troublesome. Some armchair
analysis below:

a) zswap (zswap_shrinker_count()): 2s of staleness looks fine. the
stats are only used to calculate the compression ratio and the ratio
scales a count that comes from a list_lru and *isn't* stale. The ratio
is an average over the whole pool, so it seems like that should be
fairly steady across 2s. A stale result doesn't seem too bad - afaict,
it is a heuristic of how zswap should get weighed against the other
shrinkers.

b) cachestat() syscall (filemap_cachestat()): seems preferable to just
rely on the 2s flusher worker. The results are returned back to
userspace and not used for any internal kernel decision-making, seems
ok to have one field in it (nr_recently_evicted) potentially be stale.
Seems better to err on the side of less frequent flushing anyways, as
the call path is invoked from unprivileged userspace and flushes the
root memcg.

c) workingset: looking at the original commits, the calculations are
estimates that don't require exact stats -

refaulting (workingset_test_recent()): commit 9b3016154c91 ("memcg:
sync flush only if periodic flush is delayed")
    Now the question: what are the side-effects of this change? The worst
    that can happen is the refault codepath will see 4sec old lruvec stats
    and may cause false (or missed) activations of the refaulted page which
    may under-or-overestimate the workingset size.  Though that is not very
    concerning as the kernel can already miss or do false activations.

shadow-node shrinker (count_shadow_nodes()): commit d4a5b369ad6d ("mm:
ratelimit stat flush from workingset shrinker")
    On further inspection it seems like we don't really need
    accurate stats in this function as it was already approximating the amount
    of appropriate shadow entries to keep for maintaining the refault
    information.

d) vmscan (prepare_scan_control()): for determining whether reclaim
can deactivate, there's this logic

                /*
                 * When refaults are being observed, it means a new
                 * workingset is being established. Deactivate to get
                 * rid of any stale active pages quickly.
                 */
                refaults = lruvec_page_state(target_lruvec,
                                WORKINGSET_ACTIVATE_ANON);
                if (refaults != target_lruvec->refaults[WORKINGSET_ANON] ||
                        inactive_is_low(target_lruvec, LRU_INACTIVE_ANON))
                        sc->may_deactivate |= DEACTIVATE_ANON;
                else
                        sc->may_deactivate &= ~DEACTIVATE_ANON;

(and same for DEACTIVATE_FILE for file-backed folios)

target_lruvec->refaults[] gets set at the end of the reclaim pass. It
stores the same lruvec_page_state() value that prepare_scan_control()
will read at the start of the next reclaim pass, which means if
reclaim passes happen more frequently than the 2s flushes (eg under
sustained/heavy memory pressure), this logic will incorrectly assume
no refaults occurred and deactivation is disabled, which afaict means
folios won't be moved from the active -> inactive list, and reclaim
will start evicting pages from the inactive list that are hot (eg more
refaults).

This is from reading the code rather than a reproducer though, so I
don't know how much this matters in practice. Unlike for the writeback
case, I don't think flushign more frequently solves the problem. It
would shrink the staleness window but not eliminate it. Maybe one
solution is to keep the deactivation state for a period of time if
refaults were observed.

If it turns out iterating the parents and updating the per-CPU
counters of the stat on updates is too expensive, perhaps it makes
sense to keep the existing rstat logic as is and have caller-side
workarounds, as only writeback and vmscan would require them.

Thanks,
Joanne

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 01/14] mm/memcontrol: Introduce cgroup.memory=tiered_limits boot parameter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new boot parameter 'cgroup.memory=tiered_limits' that enables tier-proportional scaling and enforcement of memory cgroup controller limits. The feature is incompatible with cgroup v1 and raises a warning if a system booted with tiered limits mounts a legacy cgroup. A static key is used to minimize overhead for cgroups not using tier-aware-memcg limits, which will become a hotpath in later commits. The patch adds code to enable the feature at boot time only, as flipping the bit at runtime could lead to uncharged or unchargeable folios.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 02/14] mm/memcontrol: Refactor page_counter charging in try_charge_memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the page_counter charging logic in try_charge_memcg to make it easier to distinguish between memcg v1 and v2 cases, in preparation for adding support for a new page_counter toptier. The changes do not introduce any functional differences, but rather simplify the code structure. This is a precursor to further modifications that will enable charging and uncharging of the new page_counter toptier.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 03/14] mm/memory-tiers: Introduce a mapping from nid to tier_slot
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new data structure called 'tier_slot' which is a dense index that maps node IDs (nid) to tiers, allowing for efficient and fixed mapping of nodes to tiers even when tiers come online or offline at runtime. The patch also adds helper functions to retrieve the nodemask associated with a tier slot. This change enables proper accounting of memory in each tier starting from boot time, addressing issues related to DAX memory hotplugging/hot-unplugging.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 04/14] mm/memcontrol: Allocate per-tier page_counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for tier-aware limits in the Linux memory controller by allocating a page_counter array per memory tier for each mem_cgroup. The array is sized to the number of node IDs and allocated only when tiered limits are enabled, reducing memory usage when the feature is off. The patch also initializes and parent-links every slot in the array during mem_cgroup allocation and frees it during mem_cgroup deallocation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 05/14] mm/memcontrol: Set tier limits proportional to memory limits
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces proportional tier limits based on memory limits when users write to memory limit sysfs files or when memory hotplug causes tier proportions to shift. The system must have tiered memcg limits enabled for this patch to take effect. It modifies the Linux kernel's memory control and memory tiers code, adding new functions and modifying existing ones to implement proportional tier limits. This change aims to improve the management of memory resources in a multi-tenant environment.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 06/14] mm/vmscan, memcontrol: Add nodemask to try_to_free_mem_cgroup_pages
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new nodemask parameter to the try_to_free_mem_cgroup_pages function in the Linux kernel's memory management subsystem. This allows selective reclaim on specific nodes, enabling future patches to target top-tier nodes and apply downward pressure when their limits are breached but global memcg-wide limits have not yet been reached. The patch modifies several files, including mm/internal.h, mm/memcontrol-v1.c, mm/memcontrol.c, and mm/vmscan.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 07/14] mm/memcontrol: Charge/uncharge tiered memory to mem_cgroup
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces tiered memory accounting to the Linux kernel's memory control group (memcg) system. It allows tracking of memory usage on a per-tier basis, where each tier represents a different type of memory. The patch adds functions to charge and uncharge memory for each tier, and updates existing code to use these new functions. This is a necessary step towards enforcing tiered limits on memory usage, which will be implemented in future patches. Currently, this only accounts for LRU folios (memory pages) and does not yet enforce tiered limits.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 08/14] mm/memcontrol: Make memory.low and memory.min tier-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch extends the existing memory.low and memory.min protection to be tier-aware, allowing for proportional best-effort and guaranteed memory protection of higher-tier memory in systems with multiple workloads isolated via the memory cgroup controller. This addresses a limitation where only total memory footprint was enforceable, not where that memory resides. The patch makes no changes unless tiered memcg limits are enabled. It modifies the include/linux/memcontrol.h and mm/memcontrol.c files to implement this new functionality.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 09/14] mm/memcontrol: Make memory.high tier-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to make the memory.high protection tier-aware, allowing for fair distribution of tiered memory among workloads in isolated memory cgroups. The existing memory.high protection is extended to consider individual tier limits and selectively reclaim on tiers when necessary.

review_comments.author: Song Hu
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue with the penalty computation in calculate_high_delay() that can overflow and produce incorrect throttling. Suggested using check_mul_overflow() to saturate the penalty instead of wrapping it.
review_comments.raw_body:
(pre-existing, not from this series - mentioning it here because
it reworks memory.high behaviour)

The penalty computation in calculate_high_delay() can overflow:

	penalty_jiffies = max_overage * max_overage * HZ;

max_overage is a fixed-point relative overage:
calculate_overage() returns (usage - high) << 20 / high, so the
square times HZ wraps once (usage - high) / high reaches
4096 / sqrt(HZ).  That is roughly 130x at HZ=1000 and 259x at
HZ=250 - reachable when memory.high is tightened far below the
current usage of a large working set.

Most wrapped values are still caught by the 2s clamp in
mem_cgroup_handle_over_high(), but residues below the clamp pass
through, and some of them produce far less throttling than
intended - down to no sleep at all.

check_mul_overflow() with a clamp would saturate the penalty
instead of wrapping it.  Could be folded in while memory.high is
being reworked, or a standalone fix.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 10/14] mm/memcontrol: Make memory.max tier-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch makes the memory.max limit in Linux's memory cgroup controller tier-aware, allowing it to enforce fair distribution of memory among workloads isolated by the controller. The existing limit is extended to consider the page counter of the tier where a folio was allocated, and reclaim is targeted at that tier's nodes when its counter exceeds the limit. This patch also updates the mem_cgroup_margin function to take into account the tier slot, ensuring that the retry check and OOM re-check under oom_lock consider the tier that actually failed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 11/14] mm/memcontrol, migrate: Transfer tier charge on migration
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a problem in the Linux kernel's memory control system where migrations across different tiers of memory allocation (per-memcg tier limits) can cause the destination tier to exceed its limit. To fix this, the patch introduces a new function `mem_cgroup_migrate_charge` that charges the destination tier separately during migration, attempting to reclaim memory if necessary and failing the migration if not enough headroom is created. The patch also updates existing functions to handle cross-tier migrations correctly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 12/14] mm/memcontrol: Kick async reclaim on migration and folio replacement
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a mechanism to kick asynchronous reclaimers when memory is being migrated or replaced, specifically in cases where soft limits are set and the system has tiered memcg limits enabled. The goal is to prevent forced charges from exceeding high memcg tier limits by triggering async reclaim. The patch adds two new functions: `tier_kick_high` which schedules a work item if the current usage exceeds the high limit, and modifies existing code in `mem_cgroup_replace_folio` and `mem_cgroup_migrate` to call this function when necessary. This approach aims to balance memory usage with soft limits without relying on synchronous reclaim.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 13/14] mm/memcontrol, sched/numa: Gate NUMA promotions into memcg tiers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new condition to gate NUMA promotions into memcg tiers, preventing unnecessary throttling of memory allocations when the destination node has sufficient headroom and the memcg tier is not at its limit. The change adds an additional check in the should_numa_migrate_memory function to consider memcg tier fullness before allowing un-ratelimited promotions. This patch only takes effect on systems with tiered memcg limits enabled, making it a targeted solution for specific use cases.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 14/14] mm/page_alloc: steer allocations away from exhausted memory tiers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's page allocator to steer allocations away from memory tiers that are exhausted, reducing unnecessary churn caused by reclaiming memory after allocation. It does this by making the page allocator aware of tier limits at allocation time and steering the first allocation attempt to nodes with available headroom in their tiered limit. This only affects movable allocations and is disabled unless tiered memcg limits are enabled.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new boot parameter 'cgroup.memory=tiered_limits' that enables tier-proportional scaling and enforcement of memory cgroup controller limits. The feature is incompatible with cgroup v1 and raises a warning if a system booted with tiered limits mounts a legacy cgroup. A static key is used to minimize overhead for cgroups not using tier-aware memcg limits, which will become a hotpath in later commits.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the need for tier-aware memory placement on systems with multiple workloads and different memory tiers. They explained that their patch introduces tiered memcg limits, which establish memory limits per-tier that scale with memcg limits and the system's per-tier capacity. The author described how these limits are enforced at allocation time, try_charge_memcg time, in the background, during migration, and through ratelimited promotions. They acknowledged that ensuring fairness in memory placement is not free and may involve underutilizing fast tiers or entering reclaim earlier to prevent overconsuming on fast tiers.
review_comments.raw_body:
INTRODUCTION
============
On machines serving multiple workloads whose memory is isolated with the
memory cgroup controller, it is currently impossible to enforce a fair
distribution of memory placement. memory.{max, high} bounds a cgroup's
total footprint but says nothing about where that memory resides, so a
cgroup that starts first can occupy all of a fast tier, while latecomers
are pushed out to slower tiers.

On systems with tiered memory (e.g. HBM, DRAM, CXL, PMEM, etc.),
memory placement directly maps to performance, meaning memory and
performance isolation breaks down on tiered systems; well-behaved
workloads using less memory than their memcg limits may still hurt other
workloads' performance by hogging more than their "fair share" of memory
on fast tiers. Performance then depends on workload-external factors,
like which other workloads are present on the system and what order they
were launched in.

However, ensuring fairness in memory placement is not free; ensuring
fair memory placement can mean underutilizing fast tiers, entering
reclaim earlier to proactively prevent overconsuming on fast tiers,
and host-level hotness inversion. On lightly-loaded systems, it means
that reclaim happens on fast tiers, even if no other workloads compete
for that memory. For some workloads, this tradeoff can be worth taking
to ensure higher run-to-run consistency and isolation from
noisy neighbors (see USECASES).

Introduce tiered memcg limits, which establish memory limits per-tier
that scale with memcg limits and the system's per-tier capacity.

MECHANISM
=========
memory.{min, low, high, max} are partitioned across the system's memory
tiers in proportion to the tiers' share of the total memory.
For instance, on a two-tier system with 75% of its memory in tier 0:
  - a cgroup with memory.max = 100G has a 75G tier 0 max limit
  - a cgroup with memory.low = 40G has 30G of tier 0 protection

Enforcement limits (high / max) are enforced in five ways:
  - At allocation time, a cgroup's allocation will try to serve a page
    from a tier where it still has headroom.
  - At try_charge_memcg time, a folio that lands on an exhausted tier
    anyways (because of __GFP_THISNODE, mempolicy, or memory pressure)
    triggers targeted reclaim restricted to that tier's nodes.
  - In the background, a tier pushed over its tiered memcg limit by page
    migration or folio replacement gets reclaimed by the memory.high
    worker.
  - Migration (promotion / demotion) now performs a try_charge on
    cross-tier migrations, and will attempt to reclaim the destination
    tier if it breaches the limits.
  - In addition, promotions are ratelimited when they are attempted on
    exhausted memcg tiers.

A few details about the enforcement:
  - Allocation time steering is best-effort and yields to explicit
    allocation requests, like mempolicy, cpusets, and allocations that
    request a specific node (promotion / demotion). If that allocation
    were to push the memcg tier over its limit, enforcement happens at
    charge time.
  - Tier max can be exceeded by demotions, which may force charge
    since they can't (and should not) trigger recursive reclaim.
  - As of this time, the mechanism is completely transparent to the
    user. Booting the system with the "cgroup.memory=tiered_limits"
    boot parameter will enable the feature, with no other interfaces.
  - There are no behavioral or performance effects on systems without
    the boot parameter, since all of the hooks are gated behind a static
    branch that compiles to a no-op. However, there are allocations and
    static variables that we must define unconditionally
    (even though they are not used).
  - Tiered memcg limits are a v2-only feature. A warning is emitted if a
    cgroup v1 user attempts to use tiered memcg limits.

USECASES
========
As mentioned in the introduction, some users may prefer to trade off
total throughput for reduced run-to-run variance:
  - VM hosting services that must provide the maximal performance
    guarantee for any workload present on a host.
  - Database workloads that want to minimize the maximum latency for
    queries hosted on the host.
  - Hosts running memory-isolated sharded workloads that block progress
    until the last shard terminates.
  - Any workload that wants to minimize variance, as a means to gather
    measurable gains in performance over time.

RFC QUESTIONS
=============
  - Should we OOM when we fail to allocate on a given tier?
  - What kinds of observability (if any) do we want?
  - What kinds of user interfaces (if any) do we want?

TESTING
=======
All the tests were run on a 1TB 2-tier 316 CPU machine, with
750G DRAM and 250G CXL. The first benchmark runs 12 containers on the
host, where each container runs an identical pointer-chasing task in a
loop. Each container is 80GB, so DRAM is overcommitted:
    (80GB * 12 = 960GB > 750GB)
I ran 8 trials and aggregated the data. When 50% of the pointers
are kept hot, these are the results:

Mean DRAM usage across the 12 workloads:
+---------+----------+--------+
|         | Untiered | Tiered |
+---------+----------+--------+
| min     | 43.09    | 51.25  |
| max     | 68.54    | 53.03  |
| max/min | 1.59x    | 1.03x  |
+---------+----------+--------+

Mean CXL usage across the 12 workloads:
+---------+----------+--------+
|         | Untiered | Tiered |
+---------+----------+--------+
| min     | 3.05     | 13.98  |
| max     | 21.65    | 14.87  |
| max/min | 7.10x    | 1.06x  |
+---------+----------+--------+

For the tiered system, the deviance from max to min DRAM and CXL usage
is quite low across workloads. What is interesting is that for untiered
systems, there is up to a 7x difference between the cgroup using the
most CXL and the least CXL; there's a clear inequality in how the
resource gets allocated.

This gets reflected in the distribution of the job completion times of
the 12 workloads as well.

Job completion time (s)
+-----------+----------+--------+-------+
|           | Untiered | Tiered | Delta |
+-----------+----------+--------+-------+
| min       |    260.1 |  276.5 | +6.3% |
| mean      |    274.4 |  290.0 | +5.7% |
| max       |    315.0 |  302.6 | -3.9% |
| max - min |     54.9 |   26.1 | -52%  |
+-----------+----------+--------+-------+

SERIES OVERVIEW
===============
Commits 1-3 are preparatory patches. We introduce the new boot
parameter, refactor try_charge_memcg() to make the following charges
easier to follow, and cache frequently-used values like the
node <-> tier mapping.

Commits 4-5 allocate the new per-memcg-tier page_counters for tracking
and set their limits according to the standard memcg limits.

Commits 6-10 track per-tier charges, and introduce the protection and
enforcement mechanisms for min/low/high/max. 

Commits 11-13 further enforce the migration (promotion / demotion) paths
and ensure that we do not introduce unnecessary churn by reclaiming
earlier. 

Commit 14 steers allocations so that we do not accidentally introduce
zone_reclaim_mode-like behavior and immediately reclaim after allocating
on exhausted memcg tiers.

FUTURE WORK
===========
I am currently working on another series [1], which pushes the memcg
cached charges (stock) to the page_counter level, meaning each tier can
manage its own independent stock. This should increase the performance
and simplicity of the code much more.

CHANGELOG
=========
v2 --> v3
- N tier support, instead of toptier vs. rest enforcement
- Max enforcement
- Migration enforcement
- Page allocator steering for exhausted tiers
- Promotion fastpath restriction & throttling

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260623180124.868655-1-joshua.hahnjy@gmail.com/

  mm/memcontrol: Allocate per-tier page_counters
  mm/memcontrol: Set tier limits proportional to memory limits
  mm/vmscan, memcontrol: Add nodemask to try_to_free_mem_cgroup_pages
  mm/memcontrol: Charge/uncharge tiered memory to mem_cgroup
  mm/memcontrol: Make memory.low and memory.min tier-aware
  mm/memcontrol: Make memory.high tier-aware
  mm/memcontrol: Make memory.max tier-aware
  mm/memcontrol, migrate: Transfer tier charge on migration
  mm/memcontrol: Kick async reclaim on migration and folio replacement
  mm/memcontrol, sched/numa: Gate NUMA promotions into memcg tiers
  mm/page_alloc: steer allocations away from exhausted memory tiers

And other code that uses pte_page() doesn't really operate on folios AFAIKs.

That's also why you are only touching hugetlb code here.

IOW, there must be a pretty good reason for us to add a non-hugetlb helper when
that looks like a good fit for common code when it's really only hugetlb that
does weird things (and doesn't need the exact page!).

If we really *need* this helper, we should spell out clearly that it is very
likely the wrong thing to use outside hugetlb code.

-- 
Cheers,

David

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 02/57] mm: add pte_none_or_zero()
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes adding a new function, pte_none_or_zero(), to the Linux kernel's mm module. The function is designed to determine whether a page table entry (PTE) maps nothing or the shared zero-page. This change aims to simplify code that needs to handle both cases by providing a single helper function.

review_comments.author: David Hildenbrand (Arm)
review_comments.summary: Identified the pte_none_or_zero() function as unnecessary and suggested using additional helpers like pte_is_zero_page() or pte_maps_zero_page().

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 03/57] mm/collapse: add collapse.h for the shared collapse state
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new header file, mm/collapse.h, which contains shared state and definitions for the collapse engine. The collapse engine is being built in its own file, and this header provides a common interface between the engine and khugepaged.c. The patch moves enum scan_result and struct collapse_control from khugepaged.c to the new header file, with no functional changes intended. This is a preparatory step for further development of the collapse engine.

review_comments.author: Lorenzo (ARM)
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that introducing a new file requires updating MAINTAINERS, specifically the THP section, and requested this change be included in the same patch.
review_comments.raw_body:
Any change that introduces a new file should in the same change update
MAINTAINERS (in the THP section to which this belongs :)

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 04/57] mm/collapse: rename mthp_present_ptes to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the 'mthp_present_ptes' bitmap to 'eligible_ptes' in the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) module. The rename is motivated by the fact that a bit being set in this bitmap does not necessarily mean the page is present, but rather that it has passed certain checks during a scan. The patch makes no functional changes and only updates the naming of the bitmap to better reflect its meaning.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 05/57] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct collapse_policy to store the policy decisions made by the caller of the collapse code. The policy is filled in once per scan pass by khugepaged and once per call by MADV_COLLAPSE. This change simplifies the collapse code by removing the need for it to look up who called it, and instead allows it to read from the stored policy. The patch also removes a NULL check in collapse_file() as it is no longer necessary.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 06/57] mm/collapse: move the smallest collapse order to collapse.h
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the definition of the smallest collapse order from khugepaged.c to a shared header file, collapse.h. This is done because the smallest collapse order is a property of collapse, not just khugepaged. The change prepares for the collapse engine, which will size its per-window arrays based on this floor. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 07/57] mm/collapse: sketch the new anonymous collapse engine
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new anonymous collapse engine to improve the scalability and functionality of memory collapsing in Linux. The current implementation is limited by its exclusive lock, which stops every fault in the address space for each huge page. The new engine addresses this issue by quiescing its sources like migration does, allowing it to run under mmap_read throughout. It also carries a batch of windows through each step together and makes decisions per window rather than per table. This patch lays out the design of the new engine without filling in the implementation details yet.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 08/57] mm/collapse: scan a table for what a collapse could use
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a table scanning mechanism to identify potential candidates for memory collapsing. The scan walks through the page table and sets a bit in the cc->eligible_ptes bitmap for each present, anonymous, non-uffd-armed, LRU, and unlocked PTE that could be used as a source for collapse. The scan takes no page table lock and produces advisory results, which are later frozen under the lock to ensure correctness. The patch also addresses issues related to partial tables, swapped-out and shared PTEs, and folio reference counts. It provides a two-sided verdict: either a PMD candidate is selected or the whole table is refused if it exceeds certain limits.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 09/57] mm/collapse: collect candidate windows into a round
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to collect candidate windows into rounds, which are batches of memory that can be collapsed together. The size of each round is capped at 32MB due to memory allocation and fault latency considerations. A dense table is collapsed as multiple rounds rather than one. The patch introduces new macros to define the maximum number of candidates per round and the batch size. It also updates the collapse_anon_pmd function to collect candidates into a round until it's full or selection is complete, then run the round and repeat the process.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 10/57] mm/collapse: run a round and feed the outcomes back
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function, collapse_round(), which runs a round of candidate evaluation and classification. The function iterates over the batch of candidates, applying passes to each one until it reaches a freeze point or the table is abandoned. The outcomes of these evaluations are then fed back into selection through the collapse_classify_result() function, allowing for decisions on what comes next in the process.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 11/57] mm/collapse: sketch the passes of a round
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new concept called 'rounds' in the collapse mechanism, which is a sequence of passes over the same batch. A round consists of three parts: before any lock, under mmap_read, and from freeze onwards. The patch lays out this sequence with stub passes for each part, including a fault-in pass that may have to sleep and drop the lock. If a fault has to wait, it is reported as SCAN_LOCK_DROPPED and the round takes the lock again and runs the pass afresh a bounded number of times.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 12/57] mm/collapse: allocate a destination per candidate
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allocates a destination per candidate in the mm/collapse mechanism. The destination is a folio of the candidate's order, charged to the memcg, and allows for deferred-split list entry while sleeping. It also introduces new functions collapse_alloc(), collapse_provision(), and collapse_deposit() to handle allocation and reclaiming of memory. The patch aims to improve the efficiency and reliability of the mm/collapse mechanism by reducing lock contention and allowing for more flexible memory management.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 13/57] mm/collapse: revalidate a round against the VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch revalidates a round against the VMA (memory area) in the Linux kernel's memory management system. It checks that the mm is not exiting and has not had THP (Transparent Huge Pages) disabled, and that the VMA still allows every provisioned candidate. The patch also finds the PTE table again to ensure it hasn't changed since the scan and allocation dropped the mmap_lock. If a VMA shrank or was replaced by a smaller one, candidates that no longer fit within its window are dropped. Finally, the patch settles the batch's span for the invalidate operation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 14/57] mm/collapse: fault the sources in before the freeze
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse functionality in the Linux kernel to fault in pages before freezing them. It ensures that each candidate slot is either a hole, the zero page, or an exclusively owned present page. The patch walks through each candidate slot and lets the fault path handle any necessary actions, such as unsharing pages shared with fork children or reading back swap entries. If a page cannot be faulted in after multiple attempts, it is left to the freeze function to refuse it. The patch also introduces a new retry mechanism for swap-in faults below the PMD order and reports dropped locks accordingly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 15/57] mm/collapse: check what a candidate would freeze
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function to check whether a candidate can be frozen in the mm/collapse module. The function walks through every slot covered by the candidate, under the table's ptl, and checks if all conditions are met for freezing. These conditions include that the folio is anonymous, not uffd-armed, and has no live mappings outside of the current span. The patch also adds a new trace event to track the scan result. If the candidate passes these checks, it can be frozen, otherwise the round only incurs the cost of the walk.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 16/57] mm/collapse: freeze the sources behind migration entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch freezes the sources behind migration entries in the Linux kernel's memory management system, ensuring that faults and GUP-slow operations wait on a folio lock taken before the first entry becomes visible. The freeze is achieved by incrementing the expected reference count of the folio, preventing new references from being acquired while the copy operation runs. This patch also includes mechanisms for restoring displaced values in case of a failed copy attempt, and ensures that writeback operations are handled correctly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 17/57] mm/collapse: copy the sources into the destinations
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, collapse_copy, which copies pages from source candidates to their corresponding destinations in memory. The copy operation is performed for each candidate that has both frozen and has a destination folio. If the source page does not exist, it is zero-filled. The function also handles machine checks on source pages and records any failures. The patch modifies the collapse_provision function to publish each destination folio in place of its corresponding sources.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 18/57] mm/collapse: install the destinations at PTE level
series_items.patch_summary: This patch installs destinations at the PTE (page table entry) level as part of a larger effort to collapse memory. It fills in the installation process for sub-PMD candidates, including verification and abort mechanisms. The verify function checks if the window is still valid to publish, while the abort function undoes frozen candidates that cannot be published due to various reasons such as machine checks or racing MADV_DONTNEED operations. The patch also includes a terminal layer for PMD-order candidates and updates the collapse.c file with new code.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 19/57] mm/collapse: install a PMD leaf as the terminal layer
series_items.patch_summary: This patch installs a PMD leaf as the terminal layer in the mm/collapse code. It does this by first verifying that the pmd is valid, then detaching the old table and depositing a fresh one under the protection of the pmd lock. The patch ensures that no pmd_none() window exists during this process, preventing faults from escaping to the pte level. This approach allows PMD collapse to run under mmap_read like other operations in the code. The patch also handles aborts and ensures that the deposited table is quiescent, while the detached table is freed after all walkers have finished.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 20/57] mm/collapse: put the sources back
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called `collapse_putback` which is responsible for putting back sources that were previously frozen during the collapse process. It iterates over each installed candidate, lowers the barriers raised by the freeze, and wakes up faulters that were sleeping on source folios' locks. The order of operations within a span is crucial: unfreeze first, then drop the rmap, unlock, and finally drop references strictly last. This patch also removes stale swapcache entries as the copy has replaced what it described.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 21/57] mm/collapse: settle whatever the round reached
series_items.patch_summary: This patch completes the last pass of a round in the collapse function, handling candidates that never froze and releasing resources held by refused candidates. It records the result for candidates that were selected but not frozen, and releases folios and tables allocated to candidates that were not installed. The patch also updates the count of installed candidates and returns this value.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 22/57] mm/collapse: walk a table with a selection cursor
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new feature to walk a table with a selection cursor, which is used to select candidate windows from the table. The cursor advances at emission and never rewinds, and it assumes that every attempt will succeed within a round. The patch also keeps track of non-present PTEs accepted by the scan in cc->scan_unmapped, adding them back only for PMD candidates. The selection process is bounded by huge page alignment and the largest enabled order.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 23/57] mm/collapse: give a refused region a second chance
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a mechanism to give refused regions in the Linux kernel's memory management system a second chance by storing them in a stack and re-probing them at a lower order. The classification of regions is based on their outcome, which can be one of four: collapse, allocation failure, refusal due to smaller window, or refusal due to in-window allocation miss. The patch also updates the `collapse_anon_pmd` function to report the outcomes of each table in order of precedence.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 24/57] mm/collapse: report each candidate's outcome to tracing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new tracepoint to the Linux kernel's tracing system, allowing the outcome of each candidate in the memory collapse process to be reported. The tracepoint provides information about the window address and order, the pass that made the decision, and the result of that decision. This allows for better understanding and debugging of the memory collapse process.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 25/57] mm/collapse: collapse anonymous memory with the new engine
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new engine to collapse anonymous memory in the Linux kernel. The old mechanism is replaced, and the new one allows collapsing of anonymous memory under mmap_read lock instead of holding mmap_write for its duration. This change improves performance by allowing faults elsewhere in the address space to continue while the collapse operation runs. Additionally, even if a table cannot be collapsed into a single huge page, the engine still identifies the largest windows within it. The patch updates several files including mm/collapse.c and mm/khugepaged.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 26/57] mm/collapse: give collapse_single_pmd() the range to work on
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse_single_pmd() function to accept a range instead of deriving it from its start point. The function is updated to pass the end of the range as an argument to both the scan and collapse operations, which already support partial tables. This change prepares for scanning VMAs that span less than a whole table and does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 27/57] mm/collapse: scan the windows a VMA can hold
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged algorithm to scan VMAs in a more efficient way by considering the largest order of windows that a VMA can hold, rather than only scanning PMD-aligned addresses. This change allows khugepaged to reach and collapse larger VMAs, including those with smaller THP orders enabled. The patch also removes unnecessary assertions and clamping logic.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 28/57] mm/collapse: remove the mechanism the engine replaces
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the mechanism that the new engine replaces in the mm/collapse code. The old anonymous collapse functionality is no longer needed as its entry point was rewired to the new engine, and all functions below it lost their last caller. The patch deletes a chain of functions including scan, mTHP order walk, collapse itself, isolation, swap-in, copy with success and failure paths, PTE release helpers, folio_pte_referenced(), and pmd-still-valid check. However, some functions like alloc_charge_folio() and hugepage_vma_revalidate() are left intact as they are still called by file paths and MADV_COLLAPSE. Four tracepoints also lose their only emitter but their definitions remain in the code.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 29/57] mm/collapse: move what a collapse is judged on into collapse.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves various functions and data from khugepaged.c to collapse.c, making the latter self-sufficient and reducing its dependency on the former. The moved functions include checks for PMD state, order calculations, and NUMA heuristics. This change aims to make the code more modular and easier to maintain.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 30/57] mm/collapse: name the max_ptes ceiling after collapse
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames a constant in the Linux kernel's memory management code to better reflect its purpose. The constant, previously named KHUGEPAGED_MAX_PTES_LIMIT, is used as a ceiling for the maximum number of page table entries (PTEs) that can be collapsed by the khugepaged process. It has been renamed to COLLAPSE_MAX_PTES_LIMIT to match other constants in the same header file and to improve clarity. The change affects several files in the kernel's memory management code, including collapse.c, collapse.h, and khugepaged.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 31/57] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to count page collapses within its own walk, rather than relying on the caller to update a shared counter. This simplifies the code and eliminates unnecessary checks for whether the collapse is being performed by the khugepaged daemon or not. The change prepares the way for moving the dispatcher into a separate file from where it can access static variables in khugepaged.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 32/57] mm/collapse: move the file collapse into collapse.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the file collapse mechanism from khugepaged.c to collapse.c, where it will be part of a unified collapse engine. The move includes functions related to file collapse, PTE-mapped THP recollapse, and table retraction. Five helpers are made static as they no longer have external callers. The patch is a pure motion of code with minimal changes, resulting in the removal of 1075 lines from khugepaged.c and addition of 1090 lines to collapse.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 33/57] mm/collapse: split collapse into a scan and a run
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the collapse functionality into two separate functions: collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd(). The scan function checks if a table needs to be collapsed, while the run function performs the actual collapse operation. This change improves lock management and reduces unnecessary lock acquisitions, making the code more efficient and easier to understand.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 34/57] mm/collapse: implement MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the implementation of MADV_COLLAPSE from khugepaged.c to madvise.c, where it belongs among other madvise operations. The move simplifies the code and removes unnecessary dependencies between the daemon's file and the syscall implementation. The patch also updates the declaration in huge_mm.h and adjusts the eligibility test for collapse. The changes do not affect the functionality of MADV_COLLAPSE itself.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 35/57] mm/madvise: drop MADV_COLLAPSE's redundant mm reference
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which holds a reference to the memory management structure (mm_struct) across its work. The reference was redundant because other parts of the code already hold references to the address space and task's memory, ensuring it remains alive during the operation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 36/57] mm/collapse: report what the scan found
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new trace event called mm_collapse_scan to report the results of an anonymous memory scan in the Linux kernel. The scan reports information such as the address scanned, the number of holes or zero-page slots, the number of swapped-out pages, and the orders that survived the scan. This information is used to determine whether a table should be refused outright or if it can still try certain orders. The patch also adds a new function called trace_mm_collapse_scan to report this information through tracing. This patch is part of a larger series of patches (36/57) and aims to improve the reporting and debugging capabilities of the kernel's memory management system.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 37/57] mm/collapse: report what the fault-in pass paid
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds reporting of faults taken during the fault-in pass in the Linux kernel's memory collapse functionality. The fault-in pass is responsible for handling swap reads and CoW breaks, but its performance was previously invisible. This patch introduces a new trace event called mm_collapse_faultin that captures the number of faults taken and their outcome. This information will help identify slow collapses or khugepaged workloads. The reporting occurs before the walk and after the mmap_lock is dropped on failure to ensure safety.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 38/57] mm/collapse: report the round, and what it made faulters wait
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new event, mm_collapse_round, to report the time it takes for a thread to wait on a source due to batching. The event includes information about the number of candidates collected and installed, as well as the outcome of the collapse operation. This is intended to help evaluate whether larger batches are beneficial by measuring the wait time for faulters. The patch introduces a new field in the trace events and updates the collapse_finish function to return the number of candidates installed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 39/57] mm/collapse: name the file collapse's tracepoints after collapse
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames two tracepoints in the Linux kernel to reflect their association with the collapse mechanism, rather than khugepaged. The renamed tracepoints are mm_collapse_scan_file and mm_collapse_file, which were previously named mm_khugepaged_scan_file and mm_khugepaged_collapse_file respectively. This change is necessary because the collapse mechanism now uses the same entry points as khugepaged, and the old names could cause issues with BPF programs that rely on these tracepoints.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 40/57] mm/collapse: remove the tracepoints of the mechanism that is gone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes four tracepoints that were no longer needed after the anonymous memory mechanism was deleted. The removed tracepoints are mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd, mm_collapse_huge_page, mm_collapse_huge_page_isolate, and mm_collapse_huge_page_swapin. These tracepoints had lost their only emitter and were no longer useful. The patch also removes two entries from the raw_tp_null_args[] array that could never match again. The engine's own events now cover the same ground as these removed tracepoints.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 41/57] mm/collapse: give collapse its own trace header
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the trace header from huge_memory.h to collapse.h, matching the new name of the kernel module that builds the tracepoints. The rename is done to better reflect the purpose and origin of the events in this header. Additionally, the enum collapse_pass is moved out of mm/collapse.h into collapse.c where the tracepoints are built. This change also updates khugepaged's selftest and other references to the old name.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 42/57] mm/collapse: allow error injection into the freeze
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows error injection into a specific function, collapse_freeze_candidate(), which is responsible for freezing memory regions during the collapse process. The goal is to test and exercise scenarios where a candidate is refused due to certain conditions, such as a co-mapper appearing between sweeps or GUP-fast pinning. The patch introduces error injection using the ALLOW_ERROR_INJECTION macro, allowing developers to simulate these refusal scenarios intentionally.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 43/57] mm/khugepaged: check the scan budget before the work, not after
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to check the scan budget before performing work, rather than after. This ensures that a pass over an address space of thousands of VMAs does not exceed the allocated budget. The changes involve adding checks for the budget at the top of both loops in the collapse_scan_mm_slot function and advancing the khugepaged_scan.address pointer when skipping a VMA to prevent walking from the same place every pass.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 44/57] mm/khugepaged: hold the address space open across a scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to hold a reference to the address space's mm_users count instead of relying on the barrier in __khugepaged_exit() and taking mmap_lock for writing. This change allows khugepaged to operate under a per-VMA lock, which does not hold mmap_lock, without causing exit_mmap() to free page tables prematurely. The patch also introduces new functions to check if an address space's owner has gone or if it is disabled from THP completely.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 45/57] mm/collapse: take a per-VMA read lock for the round
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse functionality to take a per-VMA read lock instead of holding the mmap_lock across multiple operations. This change allows writers in other parts of the mm to proceed without waiting for the collapse operation, which can be lengthy. The patch also introduces a new error code SCAN_VMA_LOCK to handle cases where the VMA is being written to and cannot be locked for reading. The collapse_revalidate function now checks if the VMA still covers the collected range after the lock has been taken.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 46/57] mm/khugepaged: scan under a per-VMA read lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to take a per-VMA read lock instead of holding the mmap_lock for the whole address space walk. This change allows multiple scans to run concurrently, improving performance. The patch also updates the cursor movement and error handling mechanisms to accommodate the new locking scheme.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 47/57] mm/madvise: collapse under a per-VMA read lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the MADV_COLLAPSE functionality in the Linux kernel to use a per-VMA read lock instead of acquiring and releasing the mmap_lock. This change allows multiple writers to access the address space simultaneously, reducing contention and improving performance. The patch also introduces new error handling for cases where the VMA cannot be locked or is being written to. Remote madvise operations are exempt from this change due to their unique requirements.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 48/57] mm/collapse: assert the mm reference the engine relies on
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse engine in the Linux kernel to assert that a reference to the mm_struct exists before performing certain operations. The patch addresses a bug where the engine was checking if the mm_users count had reached zero, which is not possible due to the way callers hold references on mm_users. Instead, it checks if collapsing has been disabled by prctl and asserts that a reference exists in other cases. This change ensures that a caller with no reference on mm_users will be detected as an error in debug builds.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 49/57] mm/khugepaged: drop the mmap_lock barrier from __khugepaged_exit()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes a redundant barrier in the __khugepaged_exit() function, which was previously taking the mmap_lock for writing and dropping it to wait for a scan holding it for reading before destroying page tables. However, since the scan now holds a reference on mm_users until its completion, it cannot be in flight at this point, making the barrier unnecessary.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 50/57] selftests/mm: attribute collapses by candidate event alone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm module to count collapses of a window by matching candidate events instead of isolate events. The recorded PFNs are no longer needed, so they have been removed from the array. This change is part of a larger series of patches and is intended to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the test.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 51/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse inside a sub-PMD VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new test cases to the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c file, which cover the collapse of memory inside a sub-page map directory (PMD) VMA. The first case tests collapsing an mTHP in a VMA that holds exactly one window, while the second case tests collapsing multiple windows within a single VMA. This patch addresses a limitation in the old mechanism, where VMAs smaller than a PMD were not considered valid collapse targets, resulting in missed opportunities for memory compaction on systems with large page sizes.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 52/57] selftests/mm: cover a hole-y window in a sub-PMD VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test case to the selftests/mm suite to cover a previously untested scenario where a partially populated window in a sub-PMU VMA is collapsed. The test checks that unfaulted slots are zero-filled and faulted pages remain unchanged after collapse. The test uses the khugepaged tool to simulate the collapse operation and verify its correctness.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 53/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse of mlocked ranges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds self-tests to cover the collapse of mlocked ranges in the Linux kernel. The tests ensure that when an mlocked range is collapsed, the source pages are properly munlocked and the new folio arrives locked as expected. The tests also verify that the collapse process works correctly under contention between threads locking and unlocking random spans across a region. The patch introduces a new function `collapse_order_mlocked` to handle this specific case of collapsing mlocked ranges.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 54/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse beside a MADV_FREE'd page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged selftest to handle a situation where one page in a PMD is marked as MADV_FREE'd, preventing the entire table from being collapsed by khugepaged. The test creates a lazyfree page and checks that the surrounding windows collapse correctly while leaving the lazyfree page intact. This ensures that reclaim can still drop the page's contents without affecting other pages in the same PMD.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 55/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse beside a pinned page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the selftests/mm/khugepaged module to cover the case where khugepaged collapses memory beside a pinned page. The test pin one page using gup_test and then checks that the rest of the table is collapsed, the window holding the pinned page is not collapsed, and the pinned page remains backed by an order-0 folio. If any of these conditions are not met, the test fails. The patch also skips the test if CONFIG_GUP_TEST or root privileges are not available.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 56/57] selftests/mm: cover the scaled max_ptes_shared limit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test case to the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c file, which covers the scaled max_ptes_shared limit. The current implementation of max_ptes_shared counts PTEs in whole PMDs but fails to account for smaller ranges that are scanned in full and judged against the same setting. This leads to incorrect results when checking if a range should collapse. To fix this issue, the patch introduces a new test case that checks both directions in one sub-PMD range with a forked child holding shared sources. The counts used in the test come from the current max_ptes_shared rather than being hardcoded, allowing the test to follow the setting and order it runs at.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 57/57] MAINTAINERS: add an entry for collapse
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes to extract the THP collapse logic into its own body of code, including a new header and tracepoint family. The existing callers, khugepaged daemon and MADV_COLLAPSE, will be updated to use the new code. Additionally, the selftests and mm_slot.h file will be moved from the THP entry to the new COLLAPSE entry in MAINTAINERS.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patchset replaces khugepaged's anonymous collapse mechanism with a new engine that can collapse sub-PMD ranges, built around migration entries and frozen folios to improve scalability and reduce disruption to the workload being collapsed. The old mechanism held the address space still by locking it, while the new engine makes the sources themselves inert between two barriers, allowing the copy to run without holding any lock. This change aims to fix limitations in the original implementation, particularly with PMD-granular operations and VMA alignment.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

Anonymous collapse is held back in two ways that its current shape cannot
be patched out of.

Functionally, an mTHP is collapsed only when the whole PMD-sized window
qualifies: collapse_scan_pmd() reaches mthp_collapse() only on
SCAN_SUCCEED.  One PTE that disqualifies itself -- uffd-armed, not
anonymous, clean lazyfree, off the LRU, pinned -- takes the whole table
with it.  A 2M range with a single such page yields nothing, even where
the half beside it would collapse perfectly well.

For scalability, collapse_huge_page() holds mmap_write across a collapse,
and anon_vma_lock_write() with it, then does the same again for the next
huge page.  Every collapse stops every fault in the address space, one
huge page at a time.

The new engine addresses both.  It quiesces its sources the way migration
does: migration entries in their PTEs, then a frozen refcount.  That is
enough to make the copy safe without the exclusive lock, so the engine
runs under mmap_read throughout.

It also carries a batch of windows through each step together, rather
than one window through all of them.  Its verdict is per window rather
than per table, so a table that cannot become one huge page still yields
the largest windows inside it.

Lay the design out first and fill it in afterwards.  What arrives here is
the shape of the engine: the two entry points, and a comment at the top
of mm/collapse.c mapping the whole call tree.  Every step below them is a
stub, filled in before the anonymous path is pointed at the engine.

collapse_scan_anon_pmd() finds the table, asks the VMA which orders it
allows, scans it, and leaves in the collapse_control what a collapse
could use.  collapse_anon_pmd() takes that range and cuts it into
windows.

The line between the two is where the lock goes.  A scan only reads a VMA
and a page table, so it keeps the mmap_lock it was called under and hands
it back.  A collapse allocates, copies and flushes, so it is called
without the lock and takes it again for each round of its own.  Nothing
then has to tell a caller whether the lock survived a call, and a caller
that finds nothing to collapse never gives the lock up at all.

Nothing calls either entry point yet; the anonymous path keeps using the
mechanism the engine replaces.

Signed-off-by: Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta) <kas@kernel.org>
